title: Scheduled and background work
grade_reasons: D, at the top of the band; the steward's reasons hold against the code and the verified findings: nearly every one of the scheduler's 13,250 calls a day finds nothing (the posts alone cost about 150 s of database time a day at the measured 11.3 ms each), all 83 dispatcher jobs share one cadence with 78 started at once on five connections, and the scheduler's log is 564 MB of a 731 MB database. The one test holds a time limit and a ledger row, never a cost, and at least 11 dispatcher jobs swallow their own errors, so the ledger says ok for them whatever happens. It is not an E: nothing here hurts a person or costs money today, and the base is sound (claimed queues, mostly set-based jobs, a ledger that emails on a failing job).
verdict_on_bar: Kept: per-store idle work at 0, a cadence and a reason per job, four jobs at a time inside 150 s, and the counters of repeated work. Loosened, because the sums did not hold: calls from 1,200 to 1,350. The steward's 1,154 leaves out the watcher and the PDF route that the plan itself adds; by the plan's own steps a quiet day is 1,274, so step 3.2's '1,200 or fewer' fails the day step 3.7 lands. Reaching 1,200 would mean an hourly watcher or no safety sweep for PDFs. Idle statements from 40,000 to 45,000: the bar's own parts add up to about 40,500 with the dispatcher at its 125, and a sweep call must run every runner without asking the gate. Otherwise the sweep of the three feature routes guards nothing, since after step 3.2 the route and the tick read the same function. Tightened: the run log from 60 MB to 25 MB once the tick runs (a week is then about 12,300 rows, 7 MB); a stopped scheduler told within 30 minutes, not an hour (an hourly watcher is 75 minutes at worst); 'no silent failure' now covers the dispatcher's jobs and not only the daily route's 19 console catches; picture re-stamps from under 100 to changes plus 20, the steward's own rule; a job starts only if its budget fits before the run's limit; a five-minute job names who waits. Added: how long due work waits, because the gate trades a poll for a predicate and nothing said the work still starts on time; the tick's own statement in the per-store budget; and a count of runs that did work, without which 'calls that take no work' cannot be read. Not measurable as written: the per-store test (its seed does not switch the features on), idle calls (no counter), and step 3.4's rg -c, which prints 6 today and not 19. Calls and statements are merged into one measure to stay at eight. The floor holds: 288 dispatcher runs always measure the status page, and 2 statements per five-minute job is the tolerance, named below. What a cron function loads at a cold start (about 11 MiB of JavaScript) is the server area's measure; it matters more here once most scheduler calls are cold sweeps.

measures.name: What a quiet day costs: function calls and statements that find nothing
measures.today: 13,250 calls a day (12,960 from nine every-minute routes, 288 dispatcher runs, 2 daily runs) and about 170,000 statements (about 68 a minute from the routes and at least 248 per dispatcher run; the auditor's count, not re-counted). The posts cost about 150 s of database time a day: 352,514 calls and 3,974 s in pg_stat_statements, 11.3 ms each.
measures.target_a: At most 1,350 calls: 288 dispatcher runs, 2 daily runs, a 15-minute sweep of each of ten gated routes (960) and the watcher every 15 minutes (96). One every-minute schedule in pg_cron, the tick, whose statement averages under 20 ms. Statements: an idle dispatcher run at most 125 (2 per five-minute job plus 9), a woken call that finds nothing at most 3, a sweep call no more than its route's count in the baseline; under 45,000 a day in all. After opening, calls that do no work stay under 1,100 a day.
measures.how_measured: Production: calls of 'SELECT net.http_post' in pg_stat_statements rise by at most 1,350 a day, kept by the daily reading of step 0.2; select count(*) from cron.job where schedule = '* * * * *' is 1; sum(runs - worked) over the route.* rows of commerce.cron_jobs (the worked count is shortfall 3). Tests: src/server/query-budget.int.test.ts (steps 1.10 and 3.3) holds the idle dispatcher run, each route's idle call and, with shortfall 1, commerce.cron_due(); src/lib/surface-budget.scan.test.ts (step 1.18) holds the number of jobs and routes.

measures.name: Jobs whose idle run does work per store, site or product
measures.today: At least 13 of the 83 dispatcher jobs (knowledge, picture vectors, alt texts, product vectors, invoices, the listings' check, the books, Tripletex, Fiken, auto-archive, autopilot budgets, recurring, eBay), 3 minute routes and the daily visits prune. Source: the planner's scan of the 83 job functions, each loop read.
measures.target_a: 0. An idle run sends the same statements and reads the same rows with 1 store and with 20, when each of the 20 has every per-store feature on (chat, pictures, an AI key of its own, open books, Tripletex, Fiken, eBay, auto-archive, an AI budget, a repeating invoice, two automations, an ad connection, a desk with email) and nothing is due. The same holds for the tick's statement. A poll of an outside service names its cap and an order that rotates.
measures.how_measured: query-budget.int.test.ts (step 1.10) on the seed and again with 19 more stores: statements, and rows read (seq_tup_read plus idx_tup_fetch). As written the step does not switch the features on and does not count the tick: shortfalls 1 and 5. src/server/cron-routes.scan.test.ts fails a per-store job without a cap and an order (step 3.3).

measures.name: Jobs that run more often than their work changes
measures.today: About 30 of the 83 dispatcher jobs run every 300 s though their work is hourly or daily: 23,904 job runs a day. Two prunes run every minute inside the integrations route, and the theme shots' wanted list is rebuilt every minute.
measures.target_a: 0. Every job names its cadence (300, 3,600 or 86,400 s) and a one-line reason in one registry. A five-minute job names who waits: a shopper, an owner, held stock or money. At most 58 jobs at five minutes and under 17,500 job runs a day with today's list. No prune runs more often than hourly.
measures.how_measured: cron-routes.scan.test.ts fails a registry job without a cadence and a reason (step 3.3). Production: select every_seconds, count(*) from commerce.cron_jobs group by 1, and runs of dispatcher.searches rising by 1 a day (288 now).

measures.name: pg_cron's own run log
measures.today: 564 MB, 77% of the 731 MB database. No retention anywhere. About 13,250 new rows a day of about 0.6 KB each (DS-8).
measures.target_a: The oldest row is at most 8 days old. The cron schema is under 80 MB while nine routes are still scheduled (a week is about 93,000 rows, 56 MB) and under 25 MB once the tick runs (about 12,300 rows a week, 7 MB).
measures.how_measured: Production: select min(end_time) from cron.job_run_details, and the size by schema in the daily reading (step 0.2). Held by the daily check of step 1.22, which fails when the oldest row is over 8 days old, and by flag four of step 1.13, which must fall from 80 MB to 25 MB when step 3.1 lands.

measures.name: Scheduled functions that are seen: a ledger row, real work recorded, no failure swallowed
measures.today: 83 dispatcher jobs and 12 routes have a row. The 40 daily functions share 2 rows and 19 of them catch to the console. At least 11 of the 83 dispatcher jobs catch an error in their entry function and neither log nor rethrow it (17 catches, by a scan of the 83 functions; runReturnJobs, runAffiliateJobs and runBonusJobs read), so the ledger says ok. Seven routes that work after answering record 0 to 1 ms. pg_cron's 2 SQL deletes have no row. No row says when a job last worked. Nothing outside pg_cron watches it.
measures.target_a: Every scheduled function, pg_cron's own SQL jobs included, has a row with its cadence, last run, last work, failures and how many runs did work. 0 catches in a job's entry function that neither rethrow nor report a failed part. A route that works after answering records that work and its failure. A stopped scheduler emails the admins within 30 minutes; a failing daily job within three days; a late daily job or a late watcher fails the status page's jobs check.
measures.how_measured: cron-routes.scan.test.ts: every function a cron route calls is a registry entry (step 3.4), and no entry function holds a silent catch (shortfall 2). rg -o 'console\.error' src/app/api/cron | wc -l prints 0 (19 today). Production: the count of daily.% rows in commerce.cron_jobs equals the registry's daily entries, and the watcher's own row is under 20 minutes old. An int test stops the tick and sees the email (step 1.22).

measures.name: Room in a run: jobs at once, time budgets, run length
measures.today: 78 jobs start at once on a pool of 5 connections with a 5 s wait; their recorded times sum to 12.1 s in a 1.3 s run. At most 16 of the 83 job modules mention a time budget. The run's limit (300 s) equals its period. The daily run starts 13 functions at once, then 8 in turn, then 19 at once, with no budget, and a function that fails waits a day.
measures.target_a: At most 4 jobs at a time, in the dispatcher and in the daily run. Every job has a budget, and a job starts only if its budget ends 15 s before the run's limit. The budgets of the fullest tick add up to at most 960 s (4 lanes of 240 s). A run stays under 150 s, and one over that is flagged slow. A daily job that failed or was not reached is tried again the same day. No run fails with 'timeout exceeded when trying to connect'. A job's cache refresh follows that job.
measures.how_measured: A unit test of runJobs() (step 3.3): never more than 4 running, a job whose budget does not fit is not started, and a job that never returns leaves the others' rows written. The scan test adds up the budgets. Production: last_duration_ms of route.cart-reminders and route.subscription-reminders, and select count(*) from commerce.cron_jobs where last_error like '%timeout exceeded when trying to connect%' is 0.

measures.name: Work repeated on things that did not change (production counters, a day)
measures.today: Empty knowledge re-cuts about 1,170. Picture vectors re-stamped about 172. issue_waiting_invoices called about 127 with no invoice issued. Every theme snapshot read 1,440 times. cookie_scans read by scan, about 21 M rows, and 40 to 50 scheduled scans where about 2 are due. Stripe payout reads 288 to 576. Up to 2,880 AI calls on listings whose answer could not be read (not measured).
measures.target_a: Each counter is at most the day's real changes plus 20: knowledge deletes no more than the pages published, picture re-stamps under 20 on a day with no upload or publish, invoice calls under 10, theme snapshot reads under 100, cookie_scans under 1 M rows read and scheduled scans at most a seventh of the sites plus 5, Stripe payout reads at most 48, and no listing asked twice in a day for the same words.
measures.how_measured: pg_stat_statements and pg_stat_user_tables a day apart, from the daily reading (step 0.2), and commerce.ai_usage where feature = 'content_moderation'. The int tests of steps 0.27 to 0.30 hold four counts. Flags two and three of step 1.13 keep watching: a table read whole, and a write that changes nothing. Three counters have no done-when today (shortfall 6): scheduled scans (0.23), snapshot reads (3.1) and payout reads (3.3).

measures.name: How long due work waits before it starts
measures.today: Not measured. The minute poll bounds it at about a minute. After the tick it is a minute while a predicate is right and up to 15 minutes when one is wrong, and nothing would say so.
measures.target_a: The oldest due row of a queue a person watches (AI page builds, looks at a page, the Dream Factory) is under 3 minutes old; of any other gated queue under 20 minutes. Over that, the admins get an email.
measures.how_measured: A function beside commerce.cron_due() returns each gated queue's oldest due row's age, from the rows' own created_at. The watcher of step 1.22 reads it every 15 minutes, and the daily reading keeps the day's worst per queue. No step makes it yet: shortfall 4.

bar_in_a_sentence: On a quiet day the scheduler makes at most 1,350 calls and 45,000 statements, none of them per store, and every job runs at the pace of its work, four at a time, inside a time budget. Every scheduled function has a ledger row that shows its work and its failures, due work starts within minutes, and a test or a daily production figure holds each of these.
can_the_steps_reach_a: No, not as written. They reach a B with step 3.3, and six small additions make it an A. The sums. Calls: 13,250 less 8,064 (step 3.1: six routes from 8,640 to 576) less 4,032 (step 3.2: three routes from 4,320 to 288) is 1,154; the watcher of step 1.22 adds 24 and the PDF route of step 3.7 adds 96: 1,274, which is 74 over the plan's own 1,200. With a 15-minute watcher it is 1,346, inside the restated 1,350. Statements: 288 x 125 = 36,000 for the dispatcher (step 3.3; the 2 a job is an estimate that the done-when enforces), about 4,900 for sweeps, 1,440 for the tick, about 400 for the daily run and the watcher: about 42,700, under 45,000. Per-store jobs: 4 by steps 0.27 and 0.28, 2 by 0.29 and 0.30, 6 by 3.6, eBay kept as a named poll; the 3 routes by 0.23 and 3.2; the visits prune by 3.4: none left. Cadence: 74 jobs at five minutes after step 0.31 and 58 after 3.3, about 17,200 job runs a day. Log: step 0.25 and then 3.1 leave about 12,300 rows a week. Where it stops short: no step ends the silent catches in at least 11 dispatcher jobs; the per-store test does not switch the features on and does not count the tick; nothing counts the runs that worked; nothing measures how long due work waits; and seven done-whens are weaker than the bar. Step 4.5 would catch the 74 calls, but not what is never measured. Two steps the ladder leaves out are needed: 1.9 (the counter step 1.10 stands on) and 1.18 (the count of jobs and routes).

shortfalls.what: Steps 3.1 and 3.2 move 'is anything due' into SQL that runs every minute, and nothing holds it. No test ties a predicate to its route's claim. The budget of step 1.10 is written before commerce.cron_due() exists and does not count it, so 'is an automation due in any store' can become one growing statement a minute, unseen. And after step 3.2 the three feature routes and the tick read the same function, so their 288 sweep calls a day guard nothing.
shortfalls.proposed_step_title: Hold the tick: its predicates, its reads and a sweep that asks no gate
shortfalls.proposed_step_what: With steps 3.1 and 3.2, S. An int test puts one claimable row in each gated queue and sees commerce.cron_due() name its route, and sees it name none on the empty seed. query-budget.int.test.ts counts the tick's statement with 1 and with 20 stores. A sweep call tells the route to run every runner's own claim without asking the due function. cron-routes.scan.test.ts fails a second every-minute schedule in supabase/migrations, and a cron route that is in neither cron_due() nor NOT_SCHEDULED.
shortfalls.proposed_done_when: The predicate test passes for all ten routes, the tick reads the same rows for 1 and for 20 seeded stores with nothing due, a scratch runner left out of the due function still runs in a sweep call, and in production the tick's statement averages under 20 ms in pg_stat_statements.

shortfalls.what: At least 11 of the 83 dispatcher jobs catch an error in their entry function and neither log nor rethrow it: 17 catches. runReturnJobs sends the reminder that a refund is past its legal deadline; if its query fails on every run, the ledger records ok for ever and no log line is written. Seven routes that work after answering record only the answer. The steward's bar counts only the daily route's 19 console catches, and no step touches the rest.
shortfalls.proposed_step_title: No job swallows its own failure
shortfalls.proposed_step_what: With step 3.3, M. The catches exist so that one part's failure does not stop the next part; keep that. runJobs() hands each job a report(error) that logs through log() and marks the run failed once its other parts have run. Each silent catch in a registry entry function is replaced with it. The after() work of the seven routes is wrapped in tracked('<route>.work'), as the Dream Factory route already does. The scan test fails an entry function with a catch that neither rethrows nor reports.
shortfalls.proposed_done_when: The scan finds 0 silent catches in the registry's entry functions (at least 11 jobs today), a unit test shows a job whose first part throws still running its second part and its row counted as failed, and an int test shows a runner that throws inside after() leaving route.page-jobs.work failed.

shortfalls.what: The bar asks that calls which do no work stay under a number, and that each row shows its last work. Step 3.3 adds only 'when a job last did any work', in its text and not in its done-when. With no count of runs that worked, idle calls cannot be read from production, and step 1.13 has no flag for them.
shortfalls.proposed_step_title: The ledger counts the runs that did work
shortfalls.proposed_step_what: With step 3.3, S. commerce.cron_jobs gains worked (runs that took at least one item) beside runs, and last_worked_at. Platform, Usage and limits shows idle runs a day per row. The daily reading of step 0.2 keeps each row's runs and worked, and step 1.13 gains a flag: idle route calls over 1,100 a day.
shortfalls.proposed_done_when: An int test shows an idle run raising runs and not worked, Usage and limits lists idle runs per job, and on a quiet day sum(runs - worked) over the route.* rows rises by at most 1,100.

shortfalls.what: The gate trades a poll for a predicate. If a predicate misses a kind of due work, that work starts up to 15 minutes late, at the sweep, and the calls figure looks better for it. A gated function is also cold when the person who waits calls it. Nothing in the plan measures how long due work waits.
shortfalls.proposed_step_title: Show how long due work waits, and say so when it is too long
shortfalls.proposed_step_what: With steps 3.1 and 1.22, S. A function beside cron_due() returns, for each gated queue, the age of its oldest due row (every queue row has created_at). The watcher reads it and emails the admins when a watched queue (AI page builds, looks at a page, the Dream Factory) is over 3 minutes, or another over 20. The daily reading keeps the day's worst per queue.
shortfalls.proposed_done_when: An int test leaves a waiting row in commerce.page_ai_jobs for 4 minutes and sees the watcher's email, and Usage and limits shows each queue's worst wait of the day.

shortfalls.what: Per-store idle work is read by running an idle tick with 1 store and with 20. Step 1.10 seeds pages and products but does not say the stores have the per-store features on. Seven of the 13 looping jobs (the books, Tripletex, Fiken, eBay, auto-archive, autopilot budgets, recurring) and the automations route loop only over stores that have the feature on, so for them the two counts would be equal today and prove nothing. The plan's note on DQ-13 also allows 2 statements a store where the bar says 0.
shortfalls.proposed_step_title: Seed the budget's stores with every per-store feature on
shortfalls.proposed_step_what: In step 1.10, S. Each of the 20 seeded stores has chat, pictures, an AI key of its own, open books, stub Tripletex, Fiken and eBay connections, auto-archive, an AI budget, a repeating invoice, two automations, an ad connection and a desk with email, with nothing due and the clock off the hour. Until steps 3.2 and 3.6 land, the difference between 1 and 20 stores is a number of its own that only falls; after them it is 0.
shortfalls.proposed_done_when: query-budget.int.test.ts lists the features its seed switches on, keeps today's difference in src/server/ratchet.baseline.json, and fails when a scratch change adds one statement per book to runLedgerPosting().

shortfalls.what: Seven done-whens stop short of the bar. 0.23: no count of scheduled cookie scans. 0.25: 'under 60 MB' is at the edge of a week's rows before the tick (about 56 MB). 1.13: flag four stays at 80 MB after the tick, when the log is about 7 MB. 1.22: no check of the SQL jobs' ledger rows; an hourly watcher means up to 75 minutes; and nothing watches the watcher, which never runs if CRON_SECRET is not set in Vercel (the review did not check). 3.1: no check of theme snapshot reads. 3.2: '1,200 or fewer' fails when step 3.7 adds a tenth route. 3.3: no check of the hourly payout read or of the budgets. 3.4: '38 or more' can pass with 15 daily functions unlisted (there are about 53 after steps 0.2, 0.31, 1.22 and 3.5), its rg -c prints 6 today and not 19, and a daily job that fails waits a day.
shortfalls.proposed_step_title: Bring seven done-whens up to the bar
shortfalls.proposed_step_what: Little new work, S. 0.23 adds: scheduled scans a day at most a seventh of the sites plus 5. 0.25 reads 'under 80 MB a week later'. 1.13: flag four falls to 25 MB when step 3.1 lands. 1.22: the watcher runs every 15 minutes, its own row and a late daily row fail the status page's jobs check, and the ledger holds a row for each pg_cron SQL job. 3.1 adds: calls of the theme snapshot statement rise by 100 or fewer a day. 3.2 reads '1,350 or fewer'. 3.3 adds: payouts.list once per mode in an hour, a job starts only if its budget fits, and the budgets of the fullest tick add up to 960 s or less. 3.4 reads 'every function the daily route calls is a registry entry', counts with rg -o, and the tick calls the daily route again, at most three times, while one of today's daily jobs has failed or not run.
shortfalls.proposed_done_when: Each of the seven steps carries its added line, and the table of step 4.5 reads every measure of this card from a named test or production figure.

tolerated: The dispatcher is called every five minutes whether or not a job is due: 288 calls a day. It always measures the status page, so no run is empty.
About 2 idle statements per five-minute job, 36,000 a day. One per job would mean folding some 30 jobs' checks into SQL, to save about 20 s of database time a day.
The 15-minute sweep: 96 calls a day per gated route that mostly find nothing. It is the net under a wrong predicate.
A gated route is cold on its first call after a quiet spell: about a second more for an owner who asks for a look at a page.
Polls of outside services that offer no push, each with a cap: eBay ten stores a run, Instagram hourly per account, carriers 60 parcels a run, Stripe payouts hourly.
CR-13: raw status checks kept 91 days, about 131,000 rows and 20 MB, the platform's own and pruned.
A failing daily job emails the admins on its third failed day, not its first. It shows as failing on the platform home from the first.
The run log keeps a week of rows: about 7 MB once the tick runs.
owner_choices: Invoice PDFs (step 3.7): made ahead by the scheduled job, so 'Try again' is true (recommended; a tenth gated route, 96 more calls a day), or made on the first download, with the route and its 102 MB function removed? The calls bar is 1,350 with it and 1,250 without.
How long are guest carts, processed webhook events and old page versions kept (step 3.5)? The daily run deletes by those periods and the privacy text states them.
How long may work that a person watches wait before the admins are told: an AI page build, a look at a page, the Dream Factory? This card assumes 3 minutes.
